title: Einstein submits final equations for his theory of gravity
dek: Albert Einstein submitted a paper to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin giving the final equations of general relativity, which treat gravity as curved space and time.
body:
In Berlin today, Albert Einstein submitted a short paper to the Prussian Academy of Sciences that sets out the finished equations of his general theory of relativity. The paper, "The Field Equations of Gravitation," links the matter and energy in any region to the curvature of space and time around it.

The submission is the fourth Einstein has made to the academy on consecutive Thursdays this month. In the earlier notes he refined the mathematics step by step. A week ago he showed that the theory explains a small extra advance in the orbit of Mercury, about forty-three seconds of arc per century, that had puzzled astronomers since the middle of the last century. The equations he handed in today drop a limiting assumption about the makeup of matter and complete the logical structure of the theory.

For generations, gravity has been understood as a force that pulls across empty space. Einstein's equations replace the force with geometry. Heavy objects bend space and time. Planets and beams of light travel along the straightest paths that the bent geometry allows. What we feel as weight or see as an orbit is the result of that bending.

Einstein was present at the meeting of the academy's physical-mathematical class and formally handed over the manuscript for printing in the proceedings. The text fills only four pages. The full reach of the result will become clear only with further study and observation.

The paper crowns years of searching. An earlier outline published with Marcel Grossmann in 1913 had to be abandoned. This autumn Einstein worked intensely, writing to David Hilbert in Göttingen, who was following a similar path. The equations recorded today meet the requirement that the laws take the same form in every coordinate system.

Clear tests remain. One prediction is that starlight grazing the Sun will be deflected by a definite angle. Astronomers expect to measure that deflection at the next suitable eclipse. Continued watching of planetary motions will supply another check.

These equations still govern our description of gravity. They keep navigation satellites accurate, describe stars orbiting black holes, and predicted the space-time ripples detected a century later. The short paper Einstein placed before the academy remains the working account of how matter shapes space and time.
